You will notice, Mr. Speaker, how the one has increased in relation to the other. I cannot understand, and I hope the minister will enlighten me as to why the government should hold down the issue of coin and currency in order to force, shall I say, people to bank money which as a rule they can only secure by borrowing. Why that is, I do not know. There is a reason why the banks can withdraw money from circulation and cause deflation or inflation, as the case may be. But we never hear anything about inflation, if it is a bank credit that is issued. On the other hand, when one talks about the government issuing currency, it is called inflation.
May I point out one thing? I said that interest could not be paid. It can be paid if there be put into circulation, without debt attached to it, the amount of interest that has to be paid each year. And so I say that all economic questions should be studied from the standpoint of the consumer, for the consumer's interests are those of the human race, and in the long run the consumer will be master.
So there is nothing -wrong with consumption. Production should be divided into three parts -machines, equipment or plant, and production by hand. Then you have labour with which to operate, supervise and maintain that plant, and you have raw material to use in your production. In the system of production there have been great changes in the last fifty years. In early history there was no doubt what production was for, because it was consumed almost as soon as it was produced. Conditions to-day, however, are different. The idea now is that production is for money, and production and consumption have become divided. The labour end of production is playing a lesser and lesser part as time goes on, because to a great extent the machine is taking the place of the worker. Something will have to be done whereby the machine which takes the work from the worker, and produces the wealth the worker would otherwise produce, must provide for the worker who has been deprived of the opportunity of producing that wealth.
There is a somewhat different problem in connection with raw material, and in some countries the problem is serious. In Canada we are most fortunate in having an abundance of raw materials, and for the benefit of succeeding generations we should be careful how the raw material is distributed. So I say, Mr. Speaker, there is nothing wrong with production, and there is nothing wrong with consumption.
But when we come to distribution, we find the greatest problem. This was emphasized again and again during the debate. Here is where we come up against what connects consumption with production, the final link between them. The purpose of all production is consumption; there is no doubt about that.

The Budget-Mr. Needham
If production and services were purchasing power, there would be no poverty in Canada; but it is the lack of this purchasing power which is the reason for many factories standing idle, and for goods being piled up, and people on relief. As I said a little while ago, this purchasing power can be withdrawn, and to a great extent between 1930 and 1934 it was withdrawn.
We listened this afternoon to an address by the hon. member for Yukon (Mrs. Black) in which she pointed to the tremendous wealth which the Yukon has produced, and the expenditures which had been incurred in that territory. But when she referred to the condition of the people there we had cause to wonder where that wealth had gone. And the same with province after province; what are we going to do about it?
I find that in 1934 Tasmania appointed a committee of their legislature to inquire into and report on subjects which I shall set out in a moment or two. These are matters we should consider. We ought to be familiar with what steps are being taken in other places to solve this serious problem. If we took the time to find out what others are trying to do, and followed the success or otherwise with which they had met, we would have a guide. The committee were to report on the following:
(1)	Whether the people are being prevented by any removable banking or financial circumstances, factor, law or condition from possessing, consuming or utilizing and enjoying the increase of wealth, or the actual increase of production over the last thirty years. And if so, the cause, and what steps should be taken to remedy it.
(2)	All matters and things pertaining and incident thereto.
The committee held meetings, examined witnesses and found that there had been great increases in actual production. They found that this increase had come with machines and fewer workers; that displaced workers were left without incomes, and that those working had lower purchasing power than in 1907; that small retailers and firms were driven out of business, and were taken over by monopolies closely identified with banks and financial institutions.
The committee's findings are as follows:
That the people are being prevented from possessing, consuming, utilizing and enjoying the increase of wealth or the increase of production over the last thirty years; that the cause of this shortage of purchasing power in the hands of the people can be effectively remedied only by,-
1.	Restoring to the sovereign community of effective control over money in all its forces;
2.	To establishment by parliament of machin-

ery which would secure regular equation between the community's production and the community's purchasing power.
That is one problem upon which we need to concentrate. We must find the equation between production and consumption. The report of the committee continues:
The opinion of the committee is that the government should control all forms of money and equality of production and purchasing power. This should be attained and maintained right through.
That is what was promised during the last election campaign in Canada. I am going to make an appeal to the Minister of Finance, because I can remember when thirty years ago west, east, and north from the homestead at Willowbrook he electrified the whole countiyside with his ideas on conditions as they then existed, and his predictions of what would come if those conditions and that system continued. He stated then that it was the duty of the federal government never to allow a shortage of legal tender money to exist; that if such a policy was permitted, debts would accumulate that never could be paid, and interest would eat up the new wealth faster than it could be created; that we would be poorer in the next twenty-five years than we were at that time. He has the chance now to make good his contention of years ago. I want to assure him that I am behind him to the utmost of my ability in every move he may make for the welfare of the citizens of this country.

Mr. Speaker, twice have I listened to the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) deliver his budget speech, and twice have I gone away filled with pride and thankfulness that in 1935 the Hon. Mr. Dunning was prevailed upon to reenter public life. We of the mari-times are proud that he chose a maritime riding for his seat. Again history repeats itself

a wise man comes from the east.
I voted against the amendment of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) not solely because I was true to my leader and to my party, but because I felt that it ill became the party of which the right hon. gentleman is the leader to try at this early date to embarrass this government regarding a problem which the last administration tried to solve for five years, only to leave it in far worse shape than they found it, and particularly when it has been clearly demonstrated that the present government is making substantial headway in its endeavours.

The Budget-Mr. Purdy
If a further amendment had been introduced against the government's wheat policy, I would have opposed it because I feel that in this matter the government is acting in the best interests of the taxpayers of Canada. When friends to my left try to make political capital out of this matter in their particular sections of the country they show little appreciation of what Canada has done and is doing for the west. It seems to me that this move is in bad taste, and my suggestion is that their short-sighted policy will have repercussions even in their own districts.
The other night the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) took occasion to refer to the Canada-United States trade agreement. He gave certain figures in connection with exports from the maritime provinces, and his conclusion seemed to be that the agreement had been of no use to the people of the maritimes. I have before me a table showing the exports of twenty-four of the principal items dealt with in the agreement for the years 1935 and 1936. I find that the value of the total exports of these twenty-four items in 1935 was $1,933,429. In 1936 the exports had increased to $3,796,885, or almost double. Yet the hon. member dares to say that an increase in trade of that proportion is of no benefit to the maritime provinces. Apparently he looked up what he had said a year ago and realized that he would have to show that he was right at that time, when he said that such a trade agreement would be of no benefit to us. I place the figures on Hansard and he can read for himself.
The hon. member claimed that the increase which has taken place in the exports of lumber to Great Britain from the maritime provinces since 1933 was due to the Ottawa agreements. I should like to place on Hansard certain figures I obtained from the Bank of Canada showing the average price in Montreal of the pound sterling for the years 1932 to 1936 inclusive. These are as follows:

1933		 4-6073
1934		 4-9891

If the hon. member will note the increase in the average price of the pound sterling, he will see that the largest increase occurred at the same time as the increase in our exports of lumber. The increase in the price of the pound sterling between 1932 and 1933 was equivalent to from $4 to $5 per thousand feet of lumber. While our lumber operators could not operate at a price of $15 per thousand feet alongside the ship, they could operate at a price of $19 or $20. The increase in
the price of the pound sterling was the reason for the increase in the exports of lumber from the maritime provinces. If my hon. friend can show me that the Ottawa agreements were responsible for the rise in the value of the pound sterling, or if he can show me that those agreements were responsible for the increased demand in Great Britain for our lumber, which has become quite marked during the last few years, I will agree with him that those agreements are all he said they were. Otherwise, I shall have to disagree.
I had intended to ask hon. members to bear with me while I attempted to change the trend of the discussion from the drought areas of the west to what I would term the forgotten areas of the east. However, as my time is limited I shall have to consign that part of my remarks to that place where so many good speeches have been consigned. While a large number of our population are engaged in fishing, lumbering and manufacturing, yet we have a large acreage of good farming land and with the same density of population as Sweden, a country very similar in climatic conditions and products, we could maintain on our land a population of approximately 1,000,000. To-day our farming population is somewhere around 230,000. I contend that in Nova Scotia we should have a forward policy to encourage the growing of more of our grains ait home. In passing, I should like to quote a statement published by the experimental farm at Nappan, as follows:
By utilizing home-grown feeds to a large extent, as outlined above, the cash outlay in rearing dairy heifers is kept at a minimum and the intelligent feeder can develop them properly to producing age at a minimum of expense.
I shall not deal further with agricultural problems this evening, but will confine myself to putting on Hansard certain facts and figures about our position. I should like to show what we have contributed to confederation and what we are doing to maintain our place in the dominion.
At the time of confederation our per capita national wealth was reported to be the highest of any of the four provinces which entered confederation. However, for the purposes of our argument I will say that it was equal. Yet in 1932, while the average per capita wealth of Canada was $2,413, that of Nova Scotia stood at $1,514, the lowest of any of the provinces.
